title: Bold Concentric Circle
scienceNote: High-contrast black boundaries on stark white trigger firing in the newborn primary visual cortex (V1).
citation: Fantz, R. L. (1961). The origin of form perception. Scientific American, 204(5), 66-72.

title: Macro Checkerboard
scienceNote: Large grid corners stimulate receptive fields of retinal ganglion cells optimized for low newborn visual acuity (~20/400).
citation: Dobson, V., & Teller, D. Y. (1978). Visual acuity in human infants. Vision Research, 18(11), 1469-1483.

title: Solid Equilateral Triangle
scienceNote: Acute vertices and wide dark surface area create strong luminance gradients that hold newborn gaze.
citation: Salapatek, P., & Kessen, W. (1966). Visual scanning of triangles by the human newborn. J. Exp. Child Psychol., 3(2), 155-167.

title: Nested Square Halo
scienceNote: Nested geometric boundaries provide multiple depth-like contours without confusing low-acuity foveal cones.
citation: Braddick, O., & Atkinson, J. (2011). Development of human visual function. Vision Research, 51(13), 1588-1609.

title: Contrast Diamond Matrix
scienceNote: Diagonal edge transitions activate orientation-selective hypercolumns in early cortical maps.
citation: Hubel, D. H., & Wiesel, T. N. (1977). Functional architecture of macaque monkey visual cortex. Proc. R. Soc. Lond. B, 198(1130), 1-59.

title: B&W Harmonic Curve
scienceNote: Opposing black and white hemispheres maximize bilateral hemispheric visual stimulation across both visual fields.
citation: Maurer, D., & Maurer, C. (1988). The World of the Newborn. Basic Books.

title: Schematic Smiling Face
scienceNote: Newborns possess an innate subcortical mechanism (Conspec) that directs immediate gaze toward face-like patterns.
citation: Johnson, M. H., et al. (1991). Newborns preferential tracking of face-like stimuli. Cognition, 40(1-2), 1-19.

title: Direct High-Contrast Gaze
scienceNote: Direct eye contact with stark contrast pupil-sclera boundaries triggers oxytocin release and stabilizes attention.
citation: Farroni, T., et al. (2002). Eye contact detection in humans from birth. PNAS, 99(14), 9602-9605.

title: Winking Schematic Face
scienceNote: Asymmetrical contrast features encourage saccadic eye movements across the midline of the face.
citation: Morton, J., & Johnson, M. H. (1991). CONSPEC and CONLERN. Psychol. Rev., 98(2), 164.

title: Parent Silhouette Profile
scienceNote: Facial profile outlines match the natural 8–12 inch feeding distance, supporting social bonding pathways.
citation: Bushnell, I. W. (2001). Mother’s face recognition in newborn infants. Infant and Child Development, 10(1-2), 51-54.

title: Crescent Happy Eyes
scienceNote: Curved brow and eye lines activate positive affective responsiveness even before conscious facial recognition.
citation: Field, T. M., et al. (1982). Discrimination and imitation of facial expressions by neonates. Science, 218(4568), 179-181.

title: Tri-Dot Face Geometry
scienceNote: Three top-heavy black marks within an oval trigger the foundational neural template for human face detection.
citation: Simion, F., et al. (2002). Newborns preference for face-like stimuli. Dev. Sci., 5(4), 427-434.

title: High-Contrast Bullseye
scienceNote: Concentric rings draw the infant’s gaze inward toward the central target point, practicing foveal fixation.
citation: Fantz, R. L. (1963). Pattern vision in newborn infants. Science, 140(3564), 296-297.

title: Radial Starburst
scienceNote: Diverging black wedges guide peripheral gaze toward the center of the visual field.
citation: Atkinson, J. (2000). The Developing Visual Brain. Oxford University Press.

title: Broad Vertical Stripes
scienceNote: Broad stripes match the spatial frequency channel (~0.5 cycles/degree) that neonates perceive most vividly.
citation: Banks, M. S., & Salapatek, P. (1978). Acuity and contrast sensitivity in 1-, 2-, and 3-month-old human infants. IOVS, 17(4), 361-365.

title: Archimedean Coil
scienceNote: Continuous spiral contours invite smooth pursuit eye movements rather than rigid discontinuous saccades.
citation: von Hofsten, C., & Rosander, K. (1996). Development of smooth pursuit tracking in young infants. Vision Research, 36(12), 1799-1810.

title: Bold Chevron Waves
scienceNote: Directional vertex arrows encourage bilateral eye coordination and spatial alignment across visual quadrants.
citation: Sireteanu, R. (2000). The development of visual cortical processing in humans. Eur. J. Neurosci., 12(7), 2139-2144.

title: Macro Polka Matrix
scienceNote: Evenly spaced dark circular disks provide structured visual landmarks that prevent infant gaze drifting.
citation: Teller, D. Y. (1979). The forced-choice preferential looking procedure. Infant Behav. Dev., 2, 135-153.

title: Panda High-Contrast Silhouette
scienceNote: Natural black-and-white patches mimic facial ocular masks, naturally anchoring infant interest.
citation: Fantz, R. L. (1961). The origin of form perception. Scientific American, 204(5), 66-72.

title: Penguin Silhouette
scienceNote: Strong vertical posture with contrasting white abdomen provides clear vertical symmetry detection.
citation: Bornstein, M. H., et al. (1981). Perception of vertical symmetry in infancy. Infant Behav. Dev., 4, 253-264.

title: Kitten Face Silhouette
scienceNote: Pointed ear contours and circular face boundary activate early feature-integration cortex.
citation: Treisman, A. (1986). Features and objects in visual processing. Scientific American, 255(5), 114-125.

title: Wide-Eyed Owl
scienceNote: Prominent concentric ocular circles strongly trigger the infant’s innate gaze-following response.
citation: Hood, B. M., et al. (1998). Eye gaze trigger for attention shifts in infants. Dev. Psychol., 34(6), 1306.

title: Gentle Baby Elephant
scienceNote: Curved trunk and rounded silhouette present large unified dark masses easy for low-acuity vision to track.
citation: Maurer, D., & Maurer, C. (1988). The World of the Newborn. Basic Books.

title: Symmetrical Butterfly
scienceNote: Bilateral wing symmetry creates balanced visual weight, easing the strain on immature ocular muscles.
citation: Humphreys, G. W., et al. (1994). Visual symmetry perception in infants. Perception, 23(1), 77-87.

title: Crimson Core Circle
scienceNote: Red wavelengths (~650nm) are the first perceived after birth as retinal L-cones mature around 6–8 weeks.
citation: Franklin, A., et al. (2005). Categorical perception of color is lateralized to the right hemisphere in infants. PNAS, 105(9), 3221-3225.

title: Red Halo Target
scienceNote: Surrounding a black disk with a vibrant red ring helps young infants differentiate chromatic from achromatic contrast.
citation: Adams, R. J., & Courage, M. L. (1998). Human infant color vision. Vision Research, 38(21), 3365-3376.

title: Ruby Prism Cross
scienceNote: Perpendicular red intersections against black gridlines challenge early parvocellular visual pathways.
citation: Livingstone, M., & Hubel, D. (1988). Segregation of form, color, movement, and depth. Science, 240(4853), 740-749.

title: High-Contrast Scarlet Heart
scienceNote: The warm red silhouette surrounded by bold black perimeter offers dual luminance-chromatic stimulus.
citation: Peeples, D. R., & Teller, D. Y. (1975). Color vision and brightness discrimination in two-month-old human infants. Science, 189(4208), 1102-1103.

title: Alternating Crimson Squares
scienceNote: Nested squares alternating black, white, and red exercise focal accommodation at 10–14 inches.
citation: Banks, M. S. (1980). The development of visual accommodation in human infants. Child Dev., 51(3), 646-666.

title: Ruby Diamond Portal
scienceNote: Sharp red corners positioned against a dark void activate parvocellular color-opponent neurons.
citation: Suttle, C. M., et al. (2002). The development of chromatic and luminance contrast sensitivity. Vision Res., 42(15), 1845-1854.

title: Cheery Blush Smile
scienceNote: Red cheek accents enhance facial saliency and stimulate emerging social smiling responses at 6–8 weeks.
citation: Sroufe, L. A., & Wunsch, J. P. (1972). The development of laughter in the first year of life. Child Dev., 43(4), 1326-1344.

title: High-Contrast Red Smile
scienceNote: A bright scarlet smile guides baby’s gaze toward the mouth, laying the visual foundation for vocal imitation.
citation: Meltzoff, A. N., & Moore, M. K. (1977). Imitation of facial and manual gestures by human neonates. Science, 198(4312), 75-78.

title: Scarlet Baby Rattle
scienceNote: A familiar circular rattle form connects tactile play experiences with high-contrast visual recognition.
citation: Streri, A., & Spelke, E. S. (1988). Haptic perception of objects in infancy. Cognit. Psychol., 20(1), 1-23.

title: Crisp Red Apple
scienceNote: The rounded red silhouette with a black leaf accent teaches figure-ground segregation.
citation: Spelke, E. S. (1990). Principles of object perception. Cognit. Sci., 14(1), 29-56.

title: Contrast Ladybug
scienceNote: Bold black polka dots on a bright red carapace present an ideal high-contrast biological visual target.
citation: Fantz, R. L. (1961). The origin of form perception. Scientific American, 204(5), 66-72.

title: Crimson Bullseye Vortex
scienceNote: Alternating rings of black, white, and scarlet create pulsating optical depth that maintains prolonged fixation.
citation: Fantz, R. L. (1965). Visual perception from birth as shown by pattern selectivity. Ann. N. Y. Acad. Sci., 118(21), 793-814.

title: Dual Chromatic Vortex
scienceNote: Complex multi-ring logarithmic spirals drive binocular foveation and motion anticipation.
citation: von Hofsten, C. (1982). Predictive reaching for moving objects by human infants. J. Exp. Child Psychol., 34(3), 439-461.

title: Concentric Infinity Tunnel
scienceNote: Progressively shrinking concentric polygons simulate 3D depth perception as stereopsis begins to emerge.
citation: Held, R., et al. (1980). Stereoacuity of human infants. Science, 209(4463), 1427-1429.

title: Primary Palette Triangle
scienceNote: By 3–4 months, S-cones (blue) and M-cones (green) join mature L-cones (red), enabling full trichromatic vision.
citation: Teller, D. Y. (1998). First glances: The vision of infants. Invest. Ophthalmol. Vis. Sci., 39(12), 2146-2156.

title: Vibrant Primary Smile
scienceNote: Multi-hued facial features prompt complex emotional categorization and infant social engagement.
citation: Nelson, C. A. (1987). The recognition of facial expressions in the first two years of life. Child Dev., 58(4), 889-909.
